text:
<margin>ṅa</margin>

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One <note>original: bhagavā</note> was staying among the Kurus, at a market town of the Kurus named Kammasadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks." "Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

"Monks, this is the direct path <note>original: ekāyano maggo; often translated as the only way or the path to the single goal</note> for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for reaching the right method, and for the realization of <term>Nibbana</term> <gloss>the cessation of suffering</gloss>, namely, the four <term>satipaṭṭhānas</term> <gloss>foundations of mindfulness</gloss>.

What are the four? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world. He dwells contemplating phenomena <note>original: dhammas; mental qualities or principles</note> in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world.

And how, monks, does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down. Having folded his legs cross legged, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.

Breathing in long, he knows, 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, he knows, 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he knows, 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, he knows, 'I breathe out short.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe in calming the bodily formation.' He trains himself, 'I will breathe out calming the bodily formation.'"

<summary>This page contains the opening of the Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta, where the Buddha declares the four foundations of mindfulness as the direct path to liberation and begins explaining mindfulness of breathing.</summary>
<keywords>Satipaṭṭhāna, mindfulness, meditation, breathing, Nibbana, Buddha, Kammasadhamma</keywords>
